## The idea

In the diffusion model, once informed always informed. Diseases are different: people recover. The SIR model, central to epidemiology since Kermack and McKendrick in 1927, tracks the **s**usceptible, the **i**nfected and the **r**ecovered. Infected people pass the disease to the susceptible people they meet, and recover at some rate. Whether the disease takes off depends on a single number, the *basic reproduction number* $R_0$: how many people one infected person infects, on average, in a fully susceptible population.

If $R_0 > 1$, each case produces more than one new case and the epidemic grows; if $R_0 < 1$, it dies out. That tipping point is why public health targets $R_0$: vaccination removes susceptible people, distancing lowers contact, and masks lower spread. Vaccinating a share $1 - 1/R_0$ of the population stops an outbreak without vaccinating everyone (herd immunity). And because spreading runs along networks, people with many contacts, *superspreaders*, matter far more than their numbers suggest.

## Formulation

::: {.model-box}
**Setup.** A population $N_{\text{POP}}$ split into susceptible $S_t$, infected $I_t$ and recovered $R_t$. Infected people make contact with probability $P_{\text{contact}}$, a contact spreads the disease with probability $P_{\text{spread}}$, and infected people recover with probability $P_{\text{recover}}$ per period.

**Equations.**

$$
I_{t+1} = I_t + P_{\text{contact}} P_{\text{spread}} \frac{I_t}{N_{\text{POP}}} S_t - P_{\text{recover}} I_t ,
\qquad
R_{t+1} = R_t + P_{\text{recover}} I_t .
$$

In the book's simplification, the recovered rejoin the susceptible pool, so $S_t = N_{\text{POP}} - I_t$; with lasting immunity, $S_t = N_{\text{POP}} - I_t - R_t$.

**Basic reproduction number.**

$$
R_0 = \frac{P_{\text{spread}} \cdot P_{\text{contact}}}{P_{\text{recover}}} .
$$

**Results.** The disease spreads if and only if $R_0 > 1$. Vaccinating a share $V > 1 - 1/R_0$ prevents spread. Without immunity, the disease settles at an endemic level $I^* = N_{\text{POP}}(1 - 1/R_0)$, or $N_{\text{POP}}(1 - V - 1/R_0)$ with a share $V$ permanently vaccinated. On a network, $R_0$ scales with $\mathbb E[k^2]/\mathbb E[k]$ rather than the mean degree, so degree inequality (superspreaders) raises it.
:::

## Interactive model

The defaults describe a disease with $R_0 = 2.5$ in a population with lasting immunity. Lower contact (distancing) to flatten the curve: the peak falls and arrives later. Raise vaccination past $1 - 1/R_0 = 60\%$ and the outbreak never starts. Switch off immunity to see the book's version, in which the disease becomes endemic.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {iterate, C, fmt, pct} from "../js/models.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof pContact = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.5, step: 0.01, label: "Contact probability P_contact"})
viewof pSpread = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.5, step: 0.01, label: "Spread probability P_spread"})
viewof pRecover = Inputs.range([0.02, 0.5], {value: 0.1, step: 0.01, label: "Recovery probability P_recover"})
viewof vacc = Inputs.range([0, 0.9], {value: 0, step: 0.05, label: "Vaccinated share V"})
viewof immunity = Inputs.toggle({label: "Recovered are immune", value: true})
```

```{ojs}
sir = {
  const N = 1e6, R0 = pContact * pSpread / pRecover;
  const start = {S: N * (1 - vacc) - 10, I: 10, R: N * vacc};
  const path = iterate(({S, I, R}) => {
    const infect = Math.min(S, pContact * pSpread * (I / N) * S), rec = pRecover * I;
    return immunity ? {S: S - infect, I: I + infect - rec, R: R + rec} : {S: S - infect + rec, I: I + infect - rec, R};
  }, start, 250).map((d, t) => ({t, S: d.S / N, I: d.I / N, R: d.R / N}));
  const peak = path.reduce((b, d) => (d.I > b.I ? d : b));
  return {path, R0, Reff: R0 * (1 - vacc), peak, end: path[path.length - 1], everInfected: immunity ? path[path.length - 1].R - vacc : NaN};
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  ariaLabel: "SIR Model: susceptible, infected and recovered over time",
  ariaDescription: "Horizontal axis: period. Vertical axis: share of the population. Lines for susceptible (teal), infected (orange) and recovered or vaccinated (purple). The summary below the chart states the result in words.",
  height: 300,
  x: {label: "Period"},
  y: {label: "Share of population", domain: [0, 1], tickFormat: "%", grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Susceptible", "Infected", "Recovered (or vaccinated)"], range: [C.teal, C.orange, C.purple]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(sir.path, {x: "t", y: "S", stroke: () => "Susceptible", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.line(sir.path, {x: "t", y: "I", stroke: () => "Infected", strokeWidth: 3}),
    immunity ? Plot.line(sir.path, {x: "t", y: "R", stroke: () => "Recovered (or vaccinated)", strokeWidth: 2}) : null
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`R₀ = ${fmt(pContact, 2)} × ${fmt(pSpread, 2)} / ${fmt(pRecover, 2)} = **${fmt(sir.R0, 2)}**${vacc > 0 ? `; with ${pct(vacc)} vaccinated the effective reproduction number is **${fmt(sir.Reff, 2)}**` : ""}. ${sir.Reff <= 1 ? `Each case causes fewer than one new case, so **the outbreak dies out**${sir.R0 > 1 ? `: vaccinating more than ${pct(1 - 1 / sir.R0)} gives herd immunity` : ""}.` : immunity ? `The epidemic peaks in **period ${sir.peak.t}** with **${pct(sir.peak.I, 1)}** of the population infected at once, and ${pct(sir.everInfected)} are eventually infected.` : `Without immunity the disease becomes **endemic**: infections settle at ${pct(sir.end.I, 1)} of the population, matching I\* = 1 − V − 1/R₀ = ${pct(1 - vacc - 1 / sir.R0, 1)}.`}`}</div>`
```

## R {.unlisted}

```{.r}
# SIR model: the book's discrete-time version, and the continuous-time
# version solved with deSolve. Deterministic: no random numbers.
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(deSolve))
p_contact <- 0.5
p_spread <- 0.5
p_recover <- 0.1
vacc <- 0 # vaccinated share
n_pop <- 1e6
r0 <- p_contact * p_spread / p_recover
cat(sprintf(
  "R0 = %.2f; herd-immunity threshold 1 - 1/R0 = %.0f%%\n",
  r0, 100 * (1 - 1 / r0)
))

# Discrete time, lasting immunity (as on the page).
s <- n_pop * (1 - vacc) - 10
i <- 10
infected <- numeric(250)
for (t in 1:250) {
  new_cases <- min(s, p_contact * p_spread * i / n_pop * s)
  recoveries <- p_recover * i
  s <- s - new_cases
  i <- i + new_cases - recoveries
  infected[t] <- i / n_pop
}
cat(sprintf(
  "Discrete: peak %.1f%% infected in period %d\n",
  100 * max(infected), which.max(infected)
))

# Continuous time with deSolve: dS = -beta S I, dI = beta S I - gamma I.
sir <- function(t, y, parms) {
  with(as.list(c(y, parms)), {
    infect <- beta * s * i
    list(c(s = -infect, i = infect - gamma * i, r = gamma * i))
  })
}
out <- ode(
  y = c(s = 1 - vacc - 1e-5, i = 1e-5, r = vacc), times = 0:250,
  func = sir, parms = c(beta = p_contact * p_spread, gamma = p_recover)
)
cat(sprintf(
  "Continuous: peak %.1f%% at t = %d; %.0f%% ever infected\n",
  100 * max(out[, "i"]), out[which.max(out[, "i"]), "time"],
  100 * (out[251, "r"] - vacc)
))

matplot(out[, "time"], out[, c("s", "i", "r")],
  type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = c("#148a91", "#d95f02", "#7570b3"),
  xlab = "Time", ylab = "Share of population"
)
```

## Takeaways

::: takeaways
- A contagion spreads only if $R_0 = P_{\text{spread}} P_{\text{contact}} / P_{\text{recover}}$ exceeds 1: a tipping point.
- Vaccinating more than $1 - 1/R_0$ of the population prevents outbreaks; distancing flattens and delays the peak.
- On networks, the spread of contacts matters: superspreaders raise $R_0$ through $\mathbb E[k^2]/\mathbb E[k]$.
:::

## Uses

::: uses
- **Act.** Set vaccination targets and evaluate distancing, masking and testing by their effect on $R_0$.
- **Predict.** Forecast the size and timing of epidemic peaks for hospital planning.
- **Explain.** Fads and behaviours that people adopt and abandon, and Page's reading of when a new corporate strategy takes hold: when enthusiasm spreads faster than it fades.
:::
